userJob: Animate something without making the page stutter
problem: Width, height, top and left are animated because they are the properties that describe the change, and each frame forces layout for the whole document
worksWhen: Any animation of position, size or presence
avoidWhen: A genuine layout change the browser must reflow anyway, which is a case for not animating it at all
mechanism: transform-performance - Use transform/opacity only; avoid animating width/height/top/left
risks: Transforms on a parent blur text in some renderers, so check the type after applying one
Promoting too many elements to their own layer, which trades jank for memory
mobileRules: A frame budget that holds on a desktop can miss on a phone; measure on the slower device
Avoid animating anything while the user is scrolling with a finger down
accessibilityRules: Under prefers-reduced-motion the transform is not applied at all rather than shortened
Transformed content stays reachable and its focus outline is not clipped
genericnessNote: A property constraint says nothing about what the motion expresses.

userJob: Decide how much of a view is allowed to move at once
problem: Every element gets an entrance, so the view arrives as a shower of independent movements and none of them means anything
worksWhen: Any view with a load or scroll-in sequence
avoidWhen: A deliberate staged reveal of a set, where the set is the subject and the stagger is the structure
mechanism: excessive-motion - Animate 1-2 key elements per view max
risks: Meeting the count by grouping ten elements into one container animation, which is the same shower in a wrapper
Choosing the moving element by convenience rather than by what should own attention
mobileRules: At 375px more of the view is one element, so a container entrance covers the whole screen; reconsider what moves
accessibilityRules: Content revealed by the animation is present and readable when motion is reduced
Nothing that moves may be the only indication that content exists
genericnessNote: A budget limits quantity, and the remaining moment still has to come from the subject rather than from the effect library.

userJob: Decide when a wait needs to be shown at all
problem: Every asynchronous call gets a spinner, so fast responses flash a loader and the interface looks unstable
worksWhen: Operations whose duration varies with the network or the server
avoidWhen: Anything near money, where the answer is a written line rather than a loader on the figure
mechanism: loading-states - Show skeleton or progress indicator when loading exceeds 300ms
risks: A skeleton whose shape does not match the loaded result, which produces a visible jump
Blanking the whole surface for a change that affects one row
mobileRules: Acknowledge locally at the row or the control rather than replacing the screen at 375px, where the screen is the context
accessibilityRules: The wait and its completion both reach a screen reader, not only the visual state
A loader does not steal focus, and focus returns to a sensible place when the wait ends
genericnessNote: A threshold governs timing, not form; a written line satisfies it as well as a skeleton.

userJob: Let a user act during an animation instead of waiting for it
problem: A transition owns the interface until it finishes, so a fast user taps into a control that has not arrived yet and the tap is lost
worksWhen: Any transition longer than a couple of frames, especially navigation and dialogs
avoidWhen: Never; a non-interruptible animation is a wait dressed as polish
mechanism: interruptible - Animations must be interruptible; user tap/gesture cancels in-progress animation immediately (Apple HIG)
risks: Cancelling mid-flight leaves the element at an intermediate value unless the end state is set explicitly
Queuing interrupted animations, so the interface catches up seconds later
mobileRules: Touch input arrives during the animation more often than pointer input does, so test the interrupt on a phone
accessibilityRules: Never block input during an animation; the interface stays operable throughout
Under reduced motion the end state is applied immediately, which makes interruption moot
genericnessNote: Interruptibility is a behavioural guarantee with no visual signature.

userJob: Decide what the page's single moment of motion is and where it comes from
problem: Motion is chosen from a library of effects, so unrelated briefs get the same reveal and the page reads as machine made because nobody chose it
worksWhen: The page genuinely carries the reader through something
avoidWhen: The page answers a question, where motion sits between the visitor and the answer
mechanism: If the page moves, that is one deliberate moment and it comes from the same nouns as the signature. Everything around it holds still. Scattered hover effects read as machine made because nobody chose them. Write the moment into the direction record with the fact it renders and the selector, before writing the code.
risks: Naming the moment after building it, which is a description rather than a decision
Spending the boldness on the moment and then adding three smaller ones anyway
mobileRules: The moment has to work at 375px or be replaced there by a static equivalent that carries the same fact
Nothing that depends on hover can be the moment, because touch has no hover
accessibilityRules: Reduced motion replaces the moment with its static end state, and the fact it renders is still readable
The moment never sits between an intent and its result
genericnessNote: Deriving the moment from the subject's nouns is what stops it converging, and the derivation has to be written down to be checkable.

userJob: Keep animation out of the path between a click and its outcome
problem: A form animates on submit and a button waits before responding, so polish is charged to the user as latency at the exact moment they are waiting
worksWhen: Every interactive surface, and hardest to hold on the ones that feel unfinished without it
avoidWhen: Never; a state change may be marked, but not by making the user wait for the mark
mechanism: Nothing moves between an intent and its result. No form animates, no click waits. Where a server is slow, the interface answers locally and states what changed in words while the figures hold still, rather than filling the gap with movement.
risks: Replacing the animation with a spinner, which is the same wait with a different shape
Answering locally and then correcting, which is worse than the original wait
mobileRules: Feedback within about 100ms of a tap, which rules out any entrance animation on the acknowledgement itself
accessibilityRules: The result is announced to assistive technology when it lands, independently of any visual transition
Focus does not move because of an animation, only because of the result
genericnessNote: A prohibition on motion in one place leaves the rest of the page's motion design open.

userJob: Use motion on an operating surface without disturbing someone doing work
problem: A console animates on scroll and on refresh, so a person reading a column of figures has the column move under them
worksWhen: Any surface someone works in for a sustained period
avoidWhen: Never on an operating surface; entertainment motion belongs on other surfaces
mechanism: Motion reports state changes only, never scroll, and it stops while anyone is typing or counting. A row that has changed may mark itself in place; the listing around it stays still. A wait past a tenth of a second is acknowledged locally rather than by blanking the surface.
risks: A live-updating list reordering itself under the pointer, which turns a click into the wrong click
Marking every update, so the mark stops meaning anything
mobileRules: At 375px an in-place mark competes with less space; prefer a word in the row over a coloured flash
accessibilityRules: A change announced through a polite live region, never an assertive one, unless it is an error
Reduced motion removes the mark's animation and leaves the changed value and its label
genericnessNote: Restricting motion to state reporting is a constraint on when, not on how it looks.

userJob: Choose one animation runtime per component tree
problem: A scroll library and a component animation library are used in the same tree, so both drive the same frames and the result is timing that cannot be reasoned about
worksWhen: Any project that needs both scroll choreography and component-level state motion
avoidWhen: A project with one runtime, where the rule costs nothing
mechanism: NEVER mix GSAP / Three.js with Motion in the same component tree. They fight over the same frames.
risks: Isolating by file rather than by tree, which does not separate the frame loop
Effect cleanup missed on unmount, which leaves a second loop running invisibly
mobileRules: Two loops on a phone shows up as dropped frames long before it does on a desktop
accessibilityRules: Whichever runtime is chosen, reduced motion must switch off the loop, not only the visible result
genericnessNote: A runtime constraint is an implementation rule with no bearing on the design's appearance.

userJob: Decide where a motion budget is best spent on a page
problem: The budget is spread across dozens of hover and micro states, so nothing is memorable and the page still costs the same to build and maintain
worksWhen: A page whose first impression carries the argument
avoidWhen: An operating surface, where a staged load delays work and motion is restricted to state reporting
mechanism: Focus on high-impact moments: one well-orchestrated page load with staggered reveals (animation-delay) creates more delight than scattered micro-interactions.
risks: A staged load that delays the first readable content, which converts the argument into a wait
Repeating the same stagger on every section, which turns one moment into a pattern
mobileRules: At 375px a staged load can push the first real content below the fold while it plays; check the first paint, not the finished state
accessibilityRules: Reduced motion renders the final composition immediately with no stagger
Nothing appears only at the end of the sequence, so an interrupted load is still complete
genericnessNote: Concentrating the budget is sound, and the staged fade-up load is itself a widely shared default, so the moment still needs a subject-specific form.
